phonemes.desc: Voiceless labiodental [f], short open-mid back [ɔ], trilled [r] — the preposition for, 'before', held brief and stressed, as in every Old Norse word.
Voiceless alveolar fricative [s] and short front [ɛ]; all three vowels of the name are short — Old Norse marks no length here.
Voiceless dental stop [t] and short close front [i]; the final -i is the weak masculine ending, so the name takes no nominative -r.

pronunciation.approximation: FOR-seh-ti — three short, even syllables, stress on the first, the r lightly trilled; close to the modern Icelandic pronunciation of forseti, 'president'.

kin.label: Old Norse
kin.form: Forseti — the theonym and the common noun forseti, 'chairman, president', a transparent compound of for, 'before', and seti, 'sitter' (cf. sitja, 'to sit')

kin.label: Old Frisian
kin.form: Fosite, the god of the island Fosetesland (Heligoland) in Alcuin's Life of Willibrord, c. 796 — the form Grimm and much modern scholarship connect with Forseti

kin.label: Younger Futhark
kin.form: ᚠᚢᚱᛋᛁᛏᛁ (f-u-r-s-i-t-i), the reconstructed Viking-Age carving; ᚢ writes the o, ᛁ writes both e and i

kin.label: Modern Icelandic
kin.form: Forseti — the god's name, and since 1944 the title of the head of state: Forseti Íslands, the President of Iceland

pronunciation.note: Forseti is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the normalized Old Norse form is already plain ASCII — no diacritic, no thorn or eth, nothing for the ASCII alphabet to lose. The name is a law-term before it is a personal name: Old Norse forseti means 'chairman, president', the one who sits before the assembly, and the god is the office made personal. Only the capital distinguishes the restored form from the input.

domains.title: Justice, Mediation
domains.subtitle: The Hall of Glitnir and the Settler of All Suits
domains.lead: Forseti is the son of Baldr and Nanna, and the quietest great office in the northern pantheon: he owns Glitnir, the hall of gold pillars and silver roof, and every quarrel that comes before him ends in peace — Snorri says all who bring their lawsuits to him go away reconciled, and Grímnismál says he dwells there day after day and puts all suits to sleep.

cards.name: Glitnir
cards.desc: 'The shining one': Forseti's hall, propped with gold and roofed with silver — the tenth dwelling in Grímnismál's tally of the homes of the gods.

cards.name: The Dómstaðr
cards.desc: The best court of judgment among gods and men — Snorri's verdict on the seat from which every party departs reconciled.

cards.name: The Spring of Fosetesland
cards.desc: The holy well on Heligoland whose water was drawn only in silence — the Frisian cult of Fosite that Alcuin records around 796.

cards.name: The Title
cards.desc: Forseti, 'he who sits before': the god's name is an office, and the office outlived the god — it is Iceland's word for its president.

symbols.name: Glitnir
symbols.meaning: The shining hall of gold pillars and silver roof — justice made architecture

symbols.name: The dómstaðr
symbols.meaning: The judgment-seat called the best among gods and men — authority measured in reconciled parties

symbols.name: Sátt, the settlement
symbols.meaning: The reconciled departure — the Edda's one statistic about Forseti: all who come with suits go away at peace

symbols.name: The silent spring
symbols.meaning: The holy water of Fosetesland, drawn only in silence — the Frisian face of the settler of strife

symbols.name: The title forseti
symbols.meaning: 'He who sits before' — the office that became a god, and the word that outlived him

mythology.lead: Forseti has the thinnest dossier of any god in the Edda with a hall to his name: one stanza in the Poetic Edda, two sentences in the Prose, and not a single adventure. What those lines build is nonetheless complete — a god whose whole mythology is the thing he does to quarrels.

myths.title: The Tenth Hall
myths.text: Grímnismál counts the dwellings of the gods, and the tenth is his: 'Glitnir is the tenth; it is propped with gold and thatched with silver too, and there Forseti dwells most days and puts all suits to sleep.' The verb is the miracle — svæfir, he lulls: not wins, not crushes, but puts to sleep, the way one settles a restless child. The poem gives him no weapon, no journey, no adversary — only a shining hall and the daily practice of ending strife.

myths.title: The Best Court Among Gods and Men
myths.text: Snorri builds the same hall twice. In the survey of the heavenly places, Glitnir stands with walls, pillars, and posts of red gold and a roof of silver. In the catalogue of the Æsir he names its owner: the son of Baldr and Nanna, daughter of Nep, is called Forseti; he owns that hall in heaven which is called Glitnir, and all who come to him with lawsuits go away reconciled — 'that is the best court of judgment among gods and men, as it is said here' — and Snorri quotes the Grímnismál stanza as his proof. The Prose Edda's whole account of the god is one sentence, and the sentence is enough: the child of the slain best of gods sits in the shining hall, and no quarrel survives him.

myths.title: The Spring on Fosetesland
myths.text: The god's name is older on parchment than the Eddas by four centuries. Around 796, Alcuin tells in his Life of Willibrord how the missionary was driven ashore on a Frisian island 'called Fosetesland after the god Fosite, whom those peoples worship' — Heligoland, the holy land. The island held a sacred spring whose water might be drawn only in silence, and the cattle that grazed there were untouchable. Willibrord baptized three men in the spring and had some of the cattle slaughtered for food; the islanders watched for the trespassers to be struck mad or dead, and when nothing happened they dragged the company before King Radbod, who cast lots daily for three days. The lot never fell on Willibrord; one of his companions was chosen and died for the sacrilege. Whether Frisian Fosite and Norse Forseti are one god remains the standing scholarly question — but the island, the silence, and the sanctity are recorded history of the cult.

myths.title: The Thirteenth Law-Speaker
myths.text: Late medieval Frisian legal texts preserve a foundation legend that Jacob Grimm could not keep away from Fosite. The Frisians, wanting law of their own, were set adrift in a boat; they prayed, and a thirteenth man appeared among the twelve law-speakers, steered them to land, threw a golden axe ashore — and where it struck, a spring burst forth — and there taught them the law. The golden axe, the spring, and the divine lawgiver made the identification irresistible to nineteenth-century scholarship; modern readers generally take the thirteenth for Christ, the usual stranger of medieval legend. The story is kept here for what it genuinely is: proof that the Frisian-speaking world remembered law as a gift that came over the water to found a thing-site by a spring.

myths.title: The Name in the Roll
myths.text: Where narrative fails, the catalogues keep him. The þulur — the mnemonic name-lists of the skaldic tradition — count Forseti in the roll of the Æsir, and Snorri's two Glitnir notices carry the hall independently of its owner. No saga stages him, no skald builds a kenning on him, and yet the name never drops out of the lists. The tradition treats him the way law treats a good judge: no stories, only the record that the court was held.

lore.syncretism: The standing cross-border question is the equation Forseti = Fosite. Jacob Grimm made it, and the philology keeps it alive: Old Norse forseti is a transparent folk-formation — 'the one who sits before' — while Frisian Fosite cannot be derived from it, which is why Lindow entertains that the Norse god was borrowed from the Frisian cult, the form attested four centuries earlier, and re-etymologized into a law-term on the way north. The Norwegian place-name Forsetlund, 'Forseti's grove', shows the name lived in Scandinavian cult-geography whatever its direction of travel. Within the corpus his true kin is Týr, the pantheon's other god of law: where Týr guarantees the oath with his right hand in the wolf's jaws, Forseti dissolves the quarrel the oath was sworn to settle. And his own house is a study in inheritance: Snorri says of Baldr that none of his judgments can stand, and of Baldr's son that no judgment of his is ever refused — the father's flaw retired in the son's office.
lore.culturalLegacy: Forseti's afterlife is the word itself. Old Norse forseti was the law-term for the presiding judge — the one who sits before the court — and when Iceland became a republic in 1944 it reached for the same word for its head of state: the President of Iceland is to this day Forseti Íslands, and no other god of the North still signs laws. In scholarship, the god's single sentence in Gylfaginning became one of the most-quoted passages on the Norse legal imagination, the standing citation for the proposition that the North idealized reconciliation over verdict. Modern Heathenry keeps him as the patron of mediation and of disputes ended without feud; and on the Frisian side, Heligoland — the holy land — still carries the memory of the cult in its name. He left no image, no saga, no drama: he left his title to a republic.
lore.extendedMeditation: Forseti is the patron of the outcome the sagas almost never reach: the quarrel that ends. The heroic literature of the North is a literature of feud — insult answered by wound, wound by killing, killing by lawsuit, lawsuit by ambush — and into that world the Edda sets one shining hall where the arithmetic stops. All who come with their cases go away reconciled: it is the only perfect record in the corpus, and it belongs to the son of the god whose own judgments could not stand. The tradition seems to know what it was asking. Reconciliation is not the absence of justice but its completion — the verdict both parties can live inside — and the god who delivers it is given nothing else: no weapon, no journey, no death, no prophecy. His silence is the teaching. In a mythology that counts its heroes by what they break, Forseti counts by what he puts to sleep.
lore.originalScriptNote: The normalized Old Norse form is Forseti — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover; in the Younger Futhark the name would have been carved ᚠᚢᚱᛋᛁᛏᛁ (f-u-r-s-i-t-i: ᚢ writes the o, ᛁ writes both e and i, and the final -i is the weak masculine ending, so the name takes no nominative ᛦ). Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered decades ago in the ordinary way: forseti.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

lore.archaeology: Forseti is a textual and onomastic god: no runestone invokes him, no image or amulet names him, and no votive deposit can be laid at his hall. The ground evidence is the place-name: Forsetlund, 'Forseti's grove', in Vestfold near the Oslo fjord, attests that the name lived in Scandinavian cult-geography and not only in Icelandic books. The Frisian witness is earlier than any Norse manuscript: Alcuin's Life of Willibrord (c. 796) preserves the island Fosetesland — Heligoland, 'holy land' — with its silent spring and sacred herd, the only near-contemporary description of the cult site of the god-name's continental form. The Norse literary witnesses are the Codex Regius (Grímnismál) and the fourteenth-century codices of the Prose Edda. The Younger Futhark rendering ᚠᚢᚱᛋᛁᛏᛁ is a normalized reconstruction of how the name would have been carved; no Viking-Age inscription of the theonym is known.
